title.narrative: UNDP - Institutional strengthening for FfD and SDGs, INFF 2021-26
UNDP - Institutionsutveckling för utvecklingsfinansiering och SDGs, INFF 2021-26

description.narrative:
The objectives of the intervention have been sligthly up-dated as part of the process of revising and updating the Theory of Change and Results monitoring framework, RMF . The main objective of the proposed up-dated programme by UNDP, is to contribute to the operationalization of the Addis Abeba Action Agenda and progress towards the SDGs at the country level.
A general comment to the up-dated programme document is that the strategic direction of the programme and implementation remains. The revision of objectives and outputs should be seen as an equation of adaptation to learnings and results and is hence adaptive management rather than major changes in direction of programming and implementation.
The proposed programme will support the operationalisation of INFFs to strengthen national financing systems in support of SDG aligned national development plans. The programme will invest in country-level processes and harness knowledge and technical capacity from the international community to help governments and their partners strengthen institutions and overcome technical bottlenecks to financing for sustainable development.
The programme has four outputs, which over the agreement period have been aligned with the overall INFF facility Joint programme framework, and hence adjusted from 3 to 4 components as compared to original agreement (already adjusted in approved workplan and budget for 2023):
1) Governments strengthen collaboration across public and private actors in operationalizing INFFs to ensure national institutional functions are in place to design and implemement inclusive financing policies and reforms.
This is focused on providing support to strengthen the institutions delivering INFFs at the national level with emphasis on building inclusive, multistakeholder approaches.
2) Countries implement financing priorities as identified through INFFs. This is focused on providing technical support and capacity development to governments and their partners at the country level as they develop and operationalize INFFs, identify entry-points and barriers for transforming their financial ecosystems, and deploy SDG financing tools to address them.
3) Governments and their partners access, share and exchange knowledge, insights and tools in support of the operationalisation of INFFs. This is focused on bringing cutting edge tools, knowledge, training, and advocacy (on policy and institutional reform, finance instruments, impact management etc) relevant to the country context.
4) Strengthened agenda setting and coherence across international partners in supporting INFFs - focused on engagement in global processes, and promoting alignment and coordination of support on SDG financing tools and technical support.
There is no change in the assessment of its contribution to Sida's vision 2023, Sida's operational plan 2022-2024 and priorities in the Strategy for Capacity Development, partnership and methods that support the 2030 agenda for Sustainable Development (goal area 1.1, 1.2 and goal area 2).
The programme is well aligned with Sida's vision 2023, the objectives set out in Sida's operational plan 2022-2024 and the priorities in the Strategy for Capacity Development, partnership and methods that support the 2030 agenda for Sustainable development. The intervention has its focus on strengthening country capacity for Financing for Development and Institution building, but aims at the same time to contribute to peer to peer learning and institutional learning at both country and global level.
The intervention has its focus on contributing to the following strategy goals:
1.1. Strengthened institutional capacity of actors in partner countries for sustainable development and poverty reduction.
1.2. Better possibilities and strengthened capacity for actors in partner countries to implment, follow up and participate in the global dialgoue on the 2030 Agenda.
The Intervention also contributes to goal area 2 of the same strategy, with focus on:
Strengthened capacity and leadership, greater knowledge and engagement among a range of actors, including Swedish actors, ability to contribute to the global implementation of the 2030 Agenda.

UNDP har inrättat en INFF - facilitet för att stödja länder att stärka de nationella finansieringssystemen till stöd för nationella utvecklingsplaner anpassade efter Agenda 2030. INFF-faciliteten kommer att genomföra insatser under en treårsperiod i en portfölj av länder. Genom faciliteten strävar UNDP efter att investera i processer på landsnivå och utnyttja kunskap och teknisk kapacitet i olika länder och från det internationella samfundet att hjälpa regeringar och deras partner att stärka institutionerna och övervinna tekniska flaskhalsar till finansiering för hållbar utveckling. INFF-faciliteten bör ses som ett sätt att samla expertutlåtanden och stödja länder på ett systematiskt och konsekvent sätt kring finansiering för utveckling. UNDP placerar partnerskap med andra FN-organ, internationella organisationer och utvecklingspartners samt inom finans- och utvecklingssektorerna som avgörande för INFF:s slutnäring.UNDP investerar i dessa partnerskap som en del av sin tjänsteleverans, i syfte att säkerställa att olika aktörer samarbetar för att stödja landsledda strategier för att finansiera hållbar utveckling. Att fördjupa och etablera partnerskap är en integrerad del av själva förändringsteorin och hörntonen i genomförandestrategin. Team Sweden kategori B. Koppling till Team Sweden och Business Sweden gjord för arbete med företagsklimat.

UNDP has established an INFF facility to support countries to strengthen national financing systems in support of SDG- aligned national development plans. The INFF Facility is set to deliver interventions over a three year period in a portfolio of countries. Through the facility, UNDP aim to invest in country-level processses and harness knowledge and technical capacity across countries and from the international community to help governments and their partners strengthen institutions and overcome technical bottlenecks to financing for sustainable development. The INFF facility should be seen as a way to gather expertice and to support countries in a systematic and coherent way around finacning for development. UNDP places partnerships with other UN agencies, international organizations and development partners as well as across the finance and development sectors as critical to the INFF endevour. UNDP invests in these partnerships as part of its service delivery, with a view to ensuring that different actors work together in support of country led approaches to financing sustainable development. Deepening and establishing partnerships is an integral part of the theory of change itself as well as the cornerstone of the implementation strategy. Team Sweden Category B. Connection to Team Sweden made through Business Sweden and working with business enabling climate.

description.narrative:
The inFF work advanced during 2025 through countries' own work, supported by the facility, but also at global meetings through for example the INFF partner meeting in Barcelona in January and the FfD 4 in Seville in the intersection of June/July.
In the current surrounding with shrinking budgets for ODA the work on INFFs is a key facility. The overarching mission of the INFF work is supporting countries in identifying, making transparent and optimzing a country's financial flows, and ultimately working for becoming independant of ODA.
Financing strategies are often the most visible output of the core INFF process, providing a strategic direction and action plan for a more sustainable national financial architecture. Governments including Egypt, Malawi and Zanzibar launched financing strategies in 2025 to support implementation across their development plans overall, while others, such as Sri Lankas Financing strategy for a just energy transition and Armenias Employment strategy, focused on financing for NDCs or sectoral and thematic priorities. This brings the total number of governments to have operationalised a financing strategy to 30, with processes advancing in 2025 in countries such as Namibia (strategy approved by Cabinet), Lesotho (strong gender equality focus), Nepal (employment focus) and Ethiopia (linked to NDC and with expected announcement of a country platform) and others expected to lead to launches in 2026.
Mobilising new finance and unlocking greater sustainable development impact
Implementation of the priorities articulated in INFFs and financing strategies already launched continued in 2025 with an emphasis on mobilising new finance and unlocking greater impact.
Public finance focused reforms yielded increases in domestic revenue and enhancements to budgetary systems for investing in sustainable development.
In Nigeria, a package of four tax bills designed to broaden the tax base, strengthen compliance, and improve equity, while building investor confidence, and with the aim of realising an 18% tax to GDP ratio in the medium term, progressed through parliament.
In Malawi, a pilot revenue management reform in Mwanza district yielded increased efficiency and receipts and will be scaled up to other municipalities.
In Zanzibar, the government mobilised $450 million from its first sukuk issuance in March 2025.
Cuba continued to rollout implementation of the program-based budgeting system prioritised through the INFF process with capacity building in key ministries and the launch of national guidelines for public policy programmes.
In Lao PDR the countrys first tax expenditure report was developed.
Lesotho built on previous gender-audits of public spending to deliver gender-budgeting reforms expected to lead toward a first annual gender budget statement in next years budget.
In Mongolia, continued rollout of SDG budgeting reforms saw growth in SDG-aligned annual public expenditure to $3 billion, up from $900 million 2 years ago.
Unlocking sustainable private investment is a crucial priority for countries within their INFFs.
In Angola, two corporate banks developed climate bond frameworks that will form the basis for issuances expected in the first half of 2025.
Maldives established a project preparation facility that has begun developing pipelines for private capital investment.
In Cabo Verde an agreement was signed with the stock exchange to deepen and expand the successful Blu-X platform, expanding the green and blue bond issuance pipeline domestically and building capacity to host cross-border issuance in the region.
Mongolia announced the development of a country platform and a solar transition fund is being piloted to mobilise private and blended capital in the energy transition.
Tanzania developed a nature investment pipeline that was promoted internationally to potential investors.
In Ghana, five assemblies established a diaspora crowdfunding and investment platform building on the local INFF process. Work to build up investment pipelines of SMEs is ongoing across five African countries, contributing for example to the Government of Congos flagship Promise un jeune, une entreprise programme to formalise up to 50,000 enterprises over five years in line with the financing strategy.
Strengthening institutions and governance of financing
Alongside reforms to unlock capital and greater impact from investment, many governments place a strong emphasis on enhancing institutional functions and governance in their INFFs. Alongside support to build capacity and capabilities in line with the financing reforms mentioned above, highlights included the strengthening of formal governance structures in countries such as Ethiopia, where INFF governance will bring together key ministries and utilise the annual business forum for structured engagement with the private sector.
In Laos a climate finance unit was established by the Ministries of Finance, and Planning and Investment, to advance implementation of the green and climate action components of the financing strategy.
Looking ahead, countries including R. Congo, Nigeria and Namibia began work on dashboards to enhance monitoring across the financing landscape and delivery of key reforms which will continue into 2026.
Informing the international agenda and strengthening partnerships
Engagement around FFD4 was a key focus in 2025. Member States reaffirmed and strengthened their commitment to INFFs, which was the most frequently mentioned initiative in the Sevilla Commitment, and with a breakthrough commitment to connect INFFs and country platforms.
A number of Sevilla Platform for Action initiatives featured INFFs, notably including Country-driven approaches to finance sustainable development and climate action.
The second phase of the INFF Facility was announced in response to Member States commitment to INFFs, in an event featuring Sidas Assistant Director-General and Senior Advisor on FFD, and with Canada announcing that they would join the INFF Facility. The Global financing playbook was launched as a practical, country-focused tool to help governments, finance institutions and development institutions scale investment.
Beyond FFD4, COP30 saw the Country Platform Hub launch including UNDP as a core partner and INFFs feature prominently in forums such as the Hamburg Sustainability Conference, G20 and LLDC3 (with INFFs now referenced in all Programmes of action, for LDCs, SIDS and LLDCs).
Facilitating peer exchange and south-south learning
The Facility continued to facilitate peer exchange between countries and with partners, the private sector and financial institutions. Beyond the side events in policy processes above, this notably included the 2025 INFF Facility Partner Meeting which brought together participants from more than 40 countries globally, and the LAC regional FFD forum, the first regional follow-up FFD4, hosted with the Government of Mexico. Overall, these exchanges provided platforms for policy makers from more than 30 countries to share experiences with peers. Knowledge products developed focused on the FFD4 process, NDC financing, local finance and other topics, as well as continuation of the Inside INFFs interview series, now featuring policymakers and finance leaders from 27 countries and a summary INFF video.
During the year an evaluation of INFF was also carried out - see Dox - giving recommendations on next stage of the facility. Sida contributed as interviewees and also on recommendations on the draft report.
In November the Program manager had the opportunity to visit Kenya and UNDP/Treasury and Ethiopia/Ministry of finance. Please see the travel report:
Kenya was in the making of engaging a new consultant, taking up from where the work landed in 2021, where the new government coming into office and adminsitration around this had slowed down the process.
Ethiopia was in the planning of launching their INFF, a process they had planned for to take place in December but had not been finalized. Ethiopia gave a thorough presentation at the Prep Com in Addis Ababa ahead of FfD in July 2024 and was preparing to make the launch soon after, but had experienced serveral delays.
A very positive development was that Canada and Spain came in as new donors to the facility, in addition to Sweden, Italy and the EU. This strengthened support increases the possibilty of reaching out to more countries, with even stronger support going forward.
In November Sida started to discuss the possibility of steering the Sida contribution towards a few countries - a suggestion that UNDP was very open to and interested in. Early contacts with Business Sweden on possibilities for making connections were also taken.
